hints: Think of what type of building blocks RNA, DNA and ATP are all built from. What is a nucleotide made of?
Compare the sugars carefully. RNA and ATP use ribose, but what sugar does DNA use? Which component stays exactly the same in all three?
walkthrough:
**Recall what these three molecules are**

All three are based on nucleotides. A nucleotide always has three parts: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group. ATP is essentially an adenine nucleotide with extra phosphates.

Remember: nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate

**Check the sugars and bases**

RNA uses ribose sugar, and ATP also uses ribose sugar. DNA is different because it uses deoxyribose sugar. The bases also vary, as DNA, RNA and ATP do not all contain adenine.

So ribose and adenosine cannot be common to all three.

**Spot the part that never changes**

Every single nucleotide in DNA and in RNA contains one phosphate group in its backbone. ATP contains three phosphate groups joined together. Hydrogen bonds hold DNA strands together, but a single ATP molecule does not rely on them as a structural component.

Conclusion: phosphate is the one component found in RNA, DNA and ATP.

options.A: Adenosine is adenine plus ribose. It is found in RNA and ATP, but DNA uses deoxyadenosine, so this is not common to all three.
options.B: Hydrogen bonds hold the two DNA strands together and occur in folded RNA, but they are not a structural component of a single ATP molecule.
options.C: Phosphate groups are present in every nucleotide of DNA and RNA, and ATP has three phosphate groups, so this is the common component.
options.D: Ribose is the sugar in RNA and ATP, but DNA contains deoxyribose instead, so ribose is not common to all three.
